h1: A beer trip to Vietnam for fresh bia hoi on the street
title: A Beer Trip to Vietnam for Fresh Bia Hoi | Craft Beer School
desc: Planning a beer trip to Vietnam around bia hoi, the fresh draught beer sold on the pavement. What it is, how to taste it and how to enjoy it sensibly.
teaser: Bia hoi is beer delivered in the morning and gone by night. Here is how to find it, taste it and read what the glass tells you.
standfirst: Bia hoi is the closest thing to a living lesson in fresh beer. It is light, cheap and made to be finished within a day or two. This guide covers what to look for and how to taste it properly on the street.
sections:
Bia hoi means "fresh beer" in Vietnamese. It is a light draught beer brewed in small local breweries and delivered in kegs, usually the same day, to pavement bars and corner restaurants. It is typically low in alcohol (commonly quoted at around 3 to 4% ABV) and served very young.

The beer is generally not pasteurised and is not built for a long life. That is the whole point. A keg that arrives in the morning is expected to be empty by closing time. The next one comes tomorrow. There is no warehouse, no long cold chain and no stale stock to sell through.

Hanoi is the city most travellers associate with it, with plastic stools low to the ground and a keg behind the counter. You will find versions of the same idea in other Vietnamese cities too, though the style and the setting change from place to place.

Most of us in India drink beer that has travelled. Even a well-run brewery sends product through a distributor, a warehouse and a shelf before it reaches a glass. Freshness is something we hope for. Bia hoi makes it ordinary.

Taste a glass and you will notice what is missing as much as what is there. There is no cardboard note from oxidation and no dull, flattened malt. Light beers are unforgiving of age because they have nothing heavy to hide behind. Our guide to fresh and stale IPA shows the same effect in a hoppier style, where the loss is even easier to hear.

The flip side is that young beer can carry green flavours. A beer that is only days old may show a faint sweet, grainy edge or a touch of fruitiness from fermentation that a longer cold rest would have cleaned up. Fresh does not mean flawless. It means honest.
How to taste it on the street

Do not expect a tasting room. Expect a small glass or a mug, a noisy road and a plate of something to eat. You can still taste with care if you slow down for the first sip.

  1. Look. It should be pale gold and clear enough to see through. A hazy glass at the end of a long day may mean the keg is nearly done.
  2. Smell. Fresh grain, a little bread and perhaps a faint hint of hop. A sour or vinegar smell means the keg has turned. Leave it.
  3. Taste. Light body, a quick finish and low bitterness. Notice how the carbonation feels. Draught lines at street bars are not always cleaned as often as a good brewpub would, so be alert to any buttery, sour or wet-paper note.
  4. Pace. Alternate with water. The low strength makes it easy to drink fast, so set your own limit before the stools get comfortable.

If you want a structured way to do this at home, our guide to beer and Indian street food uses the same habit of tasting beside a plate.

Bia hoi is built for eating beside. Small plates of grilled meat, fried spring rolls, peanuts, herbs and dipping sauces are the usual company. Fat, salt and a little chilli heat suit a light, fizzy beer because the carbonation and low bitterness clear the palate between bites.

The climate matters too. Hanoi in summer is hot and humid, like much of coastal India. A beer at 4% ABV served cold is part of why the format works there. A heavy, hoppy ale in the same heat would be hard going. That is a useful reminder for any Indian brewer designing a summer beer.

Drink only in places that look busy, where the kegs are clearly turning over. Keep an eye on the ice, the water and the glassware, as you would anywhere you travel.

You do not need a brewery tour guide. You do need a plan for the day.

  • Go in the late afternoon or early evening, before the day's kegs run low.
  • Eat first, or order food with the first round.
  • Carry small change and agree the price before you sit down. Prices are low but vary from place to place, so ask.
  • Check local rules on alcohol, opening hours and travel advice for the season before you go.
  • Arrange a safe way home. Never drive or ride a hired motorbike after drinking.

If you only visit one or two spots, pick one busy pavement bar and one more formal craft beer bar. The contrast between a beer made for tomorrow and a beer made to be shipped is the best tasting lesson of the trip.

You cannot carry bia hoi in your bag. What you can carry is the habit of asking how old a beer is. In India, ask your local bar or bottle shop when the beer was packaged. If you pour at home, our note on keeping the last glass fresh at a house party covers the basics of temperature, pouring and storage.

The deeper skill is learning to taste what has gone wrong or right in a beer without being told. On a short trip you can notice freshness. To name a fault and trace it to a cause, you need practice with a trained panel.
faqs: Is bia hoi safe to drink?
Choose busy places with fast-moving kegs, clean glasses and a cold, fresh-smelling pour. If a keg smells sour or vinegary, leave it. Use the same common sense you would apply to any street food.
It is a light beer, commonly quoted at around 3 to 4% ABV, though strength varies between breweries. Drink at your own pace and alternate with water.
Why is bia hoi not available in India?
It is made for local, same-day sale and does not travel or keep well. Packaged beer needs pasteurisation, filtration or very careful cold-chain handling to last, which is a different product.
Can I taste beer like a judge on a trip?
Yes, in a simple way. Look, smell, taste and note one thing you liked and one thing you did not. A structured course helps you put names to what you find.
